# Dhaniya Sutta (Snp 1.2 (PTS Snp 3))

**ID:** Snp 1.2 (PTS Snp 3)
**Section:** Suttanipāta (snp)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-2
**Title (Pali):** Dhaniya Sutta
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** With Dhaniya the Cowherd
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/snp1.2
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0505m.mul0.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Dhaniya Sutta* (Snp 1.2, verses 18–34) is the second discourse of the Uragavagga in the *Suttanipāta* [Hazra 1994; Norman 1997-2001]. Described as a "pastoral ballad" and a living dialogue rather than a conventional question-and-answer exchange, the text consists of alternating verses spoken by the wealthy cattle-farmer Dhaniya and the Buddha [Katre 1931; Norman 1997-2001]. The verses are composed in Vaitālīya and Aupacchandasaka metres, with hypermetric reciter's phrases (*iti Dhaniyo gopo*, *iti Bhagavā*) inserted to designate each speaker [Kingsbury 2002]. Dhaniya proclaims his contentment, domestic happiness, and physical security against the oncoming monsoon rains, while the Buddha responds in parallel, punning stanzas that reframe Dhaniya's worldly imagery into expressions of spiritual freedom, non-dependence, and homelessness [SuttaCentral; Norman 1997-2001; Johansson; Winternitz 1933]. After a torrential downpour shatters Dhaniya's reliance on material security, he and his wife seek refuge in the Buddha [Johansson; Hazra 1994]. Text-critical analysis suggests that stanzas 20–21 may reflect a textual loss, and the closing verses featuring an exchange between the Buddha and Māra represent a distinct secondary addition [Norman 1997-2001; Katre 1931].

According to SuttaCentral, passage-level parallels are found in the *Saṃyutta Nikāya* (*Nandatisutta*, SN 1.12 and SN 4.8) and their Chinese *Saṃyuktāgama* counterparts (SĀ 1004 and SĀ2 142) [SuttaCentral]. The sutta is explicitly cited or discussed in post-canonical and paracanonical works including the *Nettippakaraṇa* (Ne 9), *Peṭakopadesa* (Pe 2), and the *Milindapañha* (Mil 5.3.12, Mil 7.2.4) [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus identifies extensive Pali text reuse with the *Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā*, the *Dīpiniyaṅgapañha* (Mil 7.2.4, agreeing with SuttaCentral's citation), and verse refrains shared with several poems in the *Theragāthā* (such as Godhika, Subāhu, Uttiya, and Girimānanda; Thag 1.51, 1.52, 1.54, 5.3) [DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus also detects minor cross-language alignments with Tibetan texts in the Tengyur (D2722 and D4155-2) [DharmaNexus].
